claim: IL-SOGP jointly learns variable stiffness and damping both between task repetitions and online within each repetition, using sparse Gaussian-process basis-vector management to reduce computational scaling and improve a tracking-and-interaction-force objective in simulation; the paper proves convergence of a convex differentiable optimization objective under stated conditions, but does not prove physical interaction stability.
claim_locator: Method description: iterative and within-iteration impedance updates
Sparse online Gaussian-process basis-vector update and deletion rules
Convergence theorem for the convex differentiable objective
epistemic_status: author-reported method, theorem, simulations, and limitations; numerical and theoretical claims are unverified outside the supplied full-text packet
problem_and_setting: Robot impedance adaptation for repeated interaction tasks in a time-varying mass-damping-spring environment, evaluated only in MATLAB simulation with a 7-DoF Franka Panda. The method targets tracking performance and compliant interaction by adapting damping and stiffness.
method_or_mechanism: IL-SOGP represents variable damping and stiffness with sparse online Gaussian processes and updates both across task iterations and within each iteration. A sparse basis-vector set admits points according to novelty residual epsilon and deletes overly similar points inherited from the previous iteration using threshold w. Reported complexity is O(N M^2), compared with O(N^3) for a full Gaussian process.
content_summary: The objective combines tracking error with integrated interaction force. A theorem establishes convergence of a convex differentiable objective when its gradient is Lipschitz and the learning rate is appropriate; this is not an interaction-stability proof. At iteration 10, objective means were 0.731 versus 0.749 in the tracking case and 0.958 versus 0.987 in the compliance case for IL-SOGP versus classical IL; variances were 0.220 versus 0.236 and 0.272 versus 0.300. Changed-task and disturbance/noise/model-uncertainty simulations report faster convergence. Stable impedance adaptation, real-time cost, richer objectives, complex environments, and physical experiments remain unresolved.
synthesis_role: Method evidence for sparse, data-driven iterative impedance adaptation and a cautionary boundary case showing that objective convergence must not be treated as interaction-stability assurance.
development_link: Supports two-timescale impedance learning with sparse basis management; motivates adding independent passivity, Lyapunov, or safety layers before physical deployment.

evidence.finding: IL-SOGP updates variable damping and stiffness across repetitions and online within each repetition.

evidence.locator: Sparse basis-vector mechanism and complexity analysis
evidence.finding: Points use novelty residual epsilon, similar prior points use threshold w, and complexity is O(N M^2) rather than O(N^3).
The theorem proves convergence of a convex differentiable objective under a Lipschitz-gradient condition and suitable learning rate, not physical-interaction stability.
Comparator and IL-SOGP objective means were 0.749 and 0.731; variances 0.236 and 0.220.
Comparator and IL-SOGP objective means were 0.987 and 0.958; variances 0.300 and 0.272.
Changed-task, disturbance, noise, and model-uncertainty tests reportedly yielded faster convergence.
Stable adaptation remains open, SOGP computation challenges real time, the objective restricts scope, and hardware remains future work.

boundary_conditions: The environment is modeled as time-varying mass-damping-spring.
Main comparisons cover ten iterations and changed tasks five.
The theorem requires convex differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, and suitable learning rate.
Optimization convergence does not imply contact stability.
Performance depends on w and epsilon.
The objective uses tracking error and integrated interaction force.
O(N M^2) cost may still be too high for real time.
assumptions: Novelty and deletion thresholds are tuned.
The theorem's convexity, differentiability, Lipschitz, and learning-rate conditions hold.
Simulation uncertainty is representative only for simulation-level conclusions.

reported: Stable impedance adaptation lacks a theoretical guarantee.
Too-low w deletes excessive information; too-high w obstructs new knowledge.
Complex environments and physical tests remain future work.
inferred: Optimization convergence cannot evidence passivity, bounded contact energy, or safety.
Simulation gains do not establish transfer to hardware dynamics, delays, limits, or contact discontinuities.
Deployment may require additional approximation and safety supervision.
